variant.stem_override: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidemia presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the jaw that began 1 hour ago. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, SpO2 97% on room air. He has a known history of well-controlled hypothyroidism on stable levothyroxine therapy, with a TSH of 2.4 mIU/L on his most recent outpatient labs. Cardiac auscultation reveals a regular rate without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. ECG shows 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads I and aVL. There are no precordial ST changes.
variant.rationale_for_variant: The only addition is a history of well-controlled hypothyroidism with a normal TSH of 2.4 mIU/L, which is a stable, treated comorbidity that does not alter the ECG pattern, the differential diagnosis, or the identification of the culprit vessel. Hypothyroidism does not cause inferior ST-segment elevation or mimic RCA occlusion, so it serves purely as a distractor. The inferior STEMI pattern (ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL) continues to point unambiguously to the right coronary artery as the culprit vessel.
